The earlier island route, for instance, saved a step: its extra plank bought an action opportunity. Restoring that kind of difference requires specifying what is saved and spent, then following the whole plan again.
A Greater Ability Is Different from More Personal Wins

Put reinforcement aside and consider a separate animal ability: Rabbit alone collects three new planks instead of two. Hedgehog still collects two. Everything else stays basic, including the shared supply.

If Rabbit performs the only collect action, the game provides four starting planks plus three new ones: seven altogether. If Hedgehog does it, the total is four plus two: six. In either plan, the collecting animal stays on the bank in round one while the other moves during that round, and both then follow the original route as soon as possible, waiting after arrival. Both plans finish in round four. The first spends six planks and leaves one; the second spends six and leaves none. Rabbit provides more material, but earns no individual victory or personal reward for the leftover plank.

Whether this ability makes decisions repetitive is another question. If Lin always collects simply because he gains one more plank, Yu may have less reason to decide who prepares. If the extra plank never helps on the actual journey, the numerical advantage may also matter less than it appears. Follow what an ability provides, whether it is useful, and which decisions it gives to which person.

Turn order should be examined separately too. In the basic game, Lin acts first and Yu can see what he actually spent before deciding. Exchanging their order changes which completed results inform a decision; it does not automatically give the three-plank ability to the other animal. Changing abilities and seats together makes it harder to tell which difference caused the result.
What Does a Third Animal Need?

Remove the animal ability and return to collecting two planks. Change the game to three-player cooperation. The third player controls Squirrel, which also starts on the bank and follows the original three-step route. Each round, Lin acts, then Yu, then the third player, once each. There are still at most four rounds. All three animals arriving gives an immediate shared win; otherwise the end of round four is a loss. The initial shared supply remains four planks. Animals may share places without blocking, and enough spare pieces are provided for three players.

Three animals need nine moves and nine planks. Starting with four leaves a shortage of five. At two per collection, at least three collect actions are needed. Nine moves plus three collect actions use exactly the twelve turns provided by three players over four rounds.

Each animal must make its own three moves and has only four turns, so each must collect once. Giving two collections to the same animal would leave it too few moves. Collection is possible only on the starting bank, so all three must collect in round one. The supply rises from four to ten. Three moves in each of rounds two, three, and four leave seven, four, and one plank respectively, and all arrive. This version is possible, but tightly restricts the sequence: there is no spare wait, and no animal can leave in round one.

In the two-player game, one animal could collect while the other moved first. Adding a third decision-maker does not automatically add workable plans. Four starting planks and two per collection are not quantities that belong to an individual player. The journey they support has grown from six moves to nine.

Changing only the three-player starting supply from four to five opens another arrangement. In round one, Rabbit moves and both others collect, leaving eight planks. All three move in round two, leaving five. All three move in round three, leaving two, with Rabbit across. In round four, Rabbit waits and the other two move, spending the last two planks and winning together. One extra starting plank reduces necessary collections from three to two and makes room for a wait.
A Calculated Advantage Must Answer a Specific Question

These comparisons identify different effects. Reinforcement costs extra material without compensation. Rabbit’s ability increases team supplies. Turn order changes what is visible before deciding. Three-player starting supplies change which action sequences are possible. They cannot all be addressed by making the numbers look similar.

Adding a plank to the three-player version makes one plan possible again; it does not establish that three people will prefer playing that way. Equal ability numbers also do not ensure that everyone feels equally involved. Later chapters on observation and revision will pursue those questions. Here we first identify what is being compared and the clear consequences of its rules.

Return to the two-player base game and make the fairness question specific: who has actions left, who can add planks, and who must wait? Map those opportunities, then hear how both people describe this attempt at cooperating.
同样到岸，为什么会有不同感受？
前面我们算过木板和行动，也比较了两人的机会。现在想象第一轮的小雨：她控制的小刺猬留在起点，小兔已经向前走了一步。单看位置，小刺猬落后；看中央木板，它的一次收集又让两只动物有希望一起到岸。同一件事可以引人留意不同的部分。
主题和感受就在这些具体动作中逐渐发生关系。它们还受到人怎样理解这局游戏、此刻关注什么的影响。
先让动作配得上名字
把白色方块叫小兔、棕色方块叫小刺猬，再画一条河，会让人更容易把移动想成过河。花一块木板走到前方相邻位置，可以解释成临时搭桥；花掉的木板放到已用区，不再回来，这个说法也和用完材料的动作相接。
但名字不能偷偷增加能力。小兔仍然每次走一步，小刺猬也一样。小兔不能因为现实中的兔子会跳，就跳过踏脚石；小刺猬也没有因为名字而走得更慢。图画帮助人理解已有动作，具体可以做什么仍要说清。
假如介绍希望玩家觉得自己在“互相帮助”，规则里就需要找到帮助怎样发生。基本版让两人共用木板：一人留在起点收集两块新木板，另一人后来也能花它们前进。这个连接已经提供了可理解的帮助行为，不需要再在卡上写“获得友情”。
玩家正在拿什么作比较？
第一轮小兔前进，小刺猬收集后，中央有五块木板。如果小雨只看两只动物的距离，她可能觉得自己落后；如果她看的是能否让两只一起完成，她可能认为这一步很有用。这些都是假设的理解，不是她必然出现的心情。
设计者可以让第二种关系更容易被看见。例如，在说明里把目标写为“两只动物都到岸”，在一次示例中接着走完后续三轮，让读者看到收集怎样支持最后一步。若画面却给最先到岸的小兔加一个巨大皇冠，人们便可能被引向基本规则中不存在的个人名次。
参照也可以来自上一局。假设两人先前都急着离岸，最后缺木板；这一次商量出收集的安排。他们可以把现在与自己之前的办法比较，看见计划的改变。是否比另一桌更快，是另一个问题。游戏没有计时排名，便不能把“我们改善了办法”和“我们超过了别人”混成同一个结果。
故事需要分到一点注意
假设每次收集后还要读一段河岸故事，里面有小动物的心愿。但玩家刚好忙着计算剩余轮数，可能只想赶快找到下一次动作。增加文字，让故事在纸上变多，不等于让故事在这次游玩中更受关注。
可以把重要意思放进已经需要注意的地方。两只动物的目标一起画在对岸，中央木板明确写成共用，示例接住“留下来收集”带来的后果。这样理解帮助关系时，不必先离开当前决定，再读一段无关奖励说明。
如果确实想留一段故事，也可以放在开局或结束之后，让人有时间读。它会影响期待或回想；那与玩家作决定时注意到什么，是不同的位置。放到结尾同样不能保证所有人愿意阅读。
一句感谢不能由规则代写
设想小林在成功后说：“还好你先收集了。”这句话可能让小雨觉得自己的贡献被看见。另一种假设是，两人只是满意地确认计算成功，没有角色对白。他们都可能理解合作目标，表达方式却不同。
如果为了确保出现感谢，把“必须夸奖伙伴”写成每轮动作，得到的首先是一项要完成的说话要求。它可能让有人更愿意说，也可能让有人只想赶紧念完。规则能安排相遇、相互需要和表达的机会，无法替人决定感情。
再看一次小刺猬留在岸边的动作。木板增加了，位置没变；画面、名称和共同目标让人把它理解为怎样的一步？先听玩家的说法，再调整你给这个动作的名字。
Why Can the Same Crossing Feel Different?

We have counted planks and actions and compared the players’ opportunities. Now imagine Yu in the first round. Her Hedgehog stays at the start while Rabbit moves one step ahead. Looking at positions, Hedgehog is behind. Looking at the shared planks, its collect action has made a successful crossing possible. The same event can direct attention toward different things.
Theme and feelings begin to connect through these concrete actions. They also depend on how somebody understands the game and what they are attending to now.
Make the action fit the name

Calling a white cube Rabbit and a brown cube Hedgehog, then drawing a river, can help someone imagine movement as crossing water. Spending a plank to reach the next adjacent position can represent a temporary bridge. Moving that plank to the used area, where it does not return, fits the idea of using up material.

The names cannot silently add abilities. Both animals still move one step at a time. Rabbit cannot jump over a stone because real rabbits jump, and Hedgehog does not move more slowly because of its name. Pictures can help explain existing actions; what a player can actually do still needs to be clear.

If the introduction hopes to evoke helping each other, the rules need an identifiable way for help to occur. In the basic game, one person can stay at the start and collect two new planks that the other can later spend to move. Sharing the supply already provides an understandable helping action. A card need not announce that the players have earned friendship.
What is the player comparing?

After Rabbit moves and Hedgehog collects in round one, five planks are available. If Yu attends only to the distance between the animals, she might feel behind. If she attends to getting both across, she might see her action as useful. These are possible interpretations, not feelings she must have.

A designer can make the second relationship easier to notice. State the goal as getting both animals across, and continue an example through the remaining three rounds so the reader sees how collecting supports the final move. If the picture instead gives the first-arriving Rabbit a huge crown, it may suggest an individual ranking absent from the rules.

A reference point can also come from a previous game. Suppose both players previously rushed away from the bank and ran short of planks. This time they discuss collecting. Comparing their current plan with their own earlier attempt can reveal an improvement. Whether they finished faster than another table is a different question. With no timed ranking, improving their plan and outperforming other people are different results.
Story needs some attention too

Suppose every collect action is followed by a passage about the animals’ wishes. Players busy counting the remaining rounds may hurry past it to find their next action. More story on the page does not establish that the story receives more attention during play.

Important meaning can instead appear where players already need to look. Show both animals’ goal on the far bank, identify the central planks as shared, and continue the example to reveal what staying to collect makes possible. Understanding the helping relationship then connects directly to the current decision.

A separate story passage could appear before play or after the ending, when people have time to read it. It can affect expectations or recollection. That is a different moment from what a player notices while choosing an action. Placing it at the end still cannot guarantee that everyone wants to read it.
A rule cannot write somebody’s gratitude

Imagine Lin saying after a win, “Good thing you collected first.” Yu might feel that her contribution was recognized. In another imagined session, both simply enjoy confirming that their calculation worked, without speaking as the animals. They may understand the same cooperative goal and express it differently.

Making “praise your partner” a required action first creates a speaking requirement. It might encourage somebody to speak, or make somebody eager to finish reciting the line. Rules can arrange encounters, mutual needs, and opportunities for expression. They cannot choose people’s feelings for them.

Look again at Hedgehog staying on the bank. The supply grew; the position stayed still. How do the picture, name, and shared goal lead someone to describe that step? Hear the player’s account before revising what you call the action.
这条河讲了什么，又省略了什么？
小动物过河让我们记住位置、木板和轮数，却没有要求判断风向、河水深浅或动物是否会游泳。它把复杂的过河情景缩成几种能看懂、能改变的关系。这样的取舍可以叫作建立模型。
模型让我们用少量东西思考一个问题。要理解它，还得看清：哪些关系写进了规则，哪些只是图画或故事，又有哪些根本没有出现。
省略以后，留下了什么问题？
基本版让每次前进花一块木板，只有仍在起点的动物能收集，第四轮末必须到齐。这些关系共同形成一个问题：谁要先留在岸上，让两只动物还有足够材料和机会走完？我们不需要知道水温，就能算这件事。
现在假设在河里画了几条鱼，介绍又写“保护河流”。若全部动作仍只改变动物位置和木板数量，玩家没有办法通过选择改变鱼的处境。图画带来了鱼，规则还没有表达保护怎样发生。
若想让保护成为真正要考虑的事，需要先决定一种关系，比如某种行动怎样影响鱼，再明确如何看到后果、它与到岸目标怎样相连。每加一种关系都可能增加要理解和记录的事情。也可以选择把鱼保留为背景，把本版明确介绍为商量共同过河。模型可以小，承诺需要和它实际表达的内容相称。
不只是省略，连起来的方法也有立场
下面暂时离开小动物，看一个完全虚构的河边消息模型。它是独立的小模型，不加入过河规则。
河边只有甲、乙、丙三户，排成一行：甲与乙相邻，乙与丙相邻，甲与丙不相邻。开始时三户都不知道一条消息。玩家有两枚通告片，每次花一枚，选一户宣读；被选中的这一户及其直接相邻住户立即知道消息。消息不会继续传下去，已经知道的人一直记得。三户都知道就立即完成，否则两枚用完便未完成。
选乙一次，乙和两边的甲、丙都知道，只花一枚就完成。先选甲，只能让甲、乙知道；再选丙才使三户到齐，共用两枚。这些结果来自我们写下的规则，可以逐步算出。
但为什么相邻就必定听到？为什么没人主动再讲给朋友？这个模型把距离写成传递条件，把宣读写成必然有效，还省略了信任、语言和其他联系。选择这些关系，使中间一户成为特别有效的位置。规则已经表达了一种看问题的方法，并非一张完全没有取舍的现实照片。
如果要用它讨论现实消息传播，便需要另外了解现实中的这些关系是否成立。这个虚构结果只证明在所写条件下会怎样，不能证明现实中的中间住户一定最有影响力。
故事可以留白，行动不能靠猜
回到过河。小刺猬为什么愿意留在岸上？可以不规定唯一答案。有人可能把它想成谨慎，有人可能想成照顾朋友。只要动作仍按同一规则执行，这块故事空白可以容纳不同理解。
“收集后木板放哪里”则不能同样留白。放进中央，两只都能用；放进个人口袋，另一只就不能直接花。这里会产生不同的下一步，需要明确规定，而不能让玩家凭动物性格猜答案。
同样，小兔和小刺猬在现实故事里可以有不同速度，本版却给它们相同的步长。这样我们能把注意放在先后安排与共享材料。名字对应的是角色形象；这份相同能力则是模型的选择。
一段回忆，也会重新选择重点
假设一局结束后有人说：“小兔一路领先，率先登岸。”句子符合那条成功路线，却漏掉了小刺猬第一轮收集。另一个说法是：“小刺猬先备好材料，两只才一起到岸。”它突出互相支持，也没有把每一步都复述一遍。
若说“小兔替大家探明了路线”，就加入了规则中没有发生的发现：基本版从开局起，路线便全部可见，小兔前进没有揭开新信息。故事可以有不同重点，涉及动作造成什么时，仍要和实际经过相接。
把希望玩家考虑的事写在地图旁，再逐项找到对应动作。没有对应动作的承诺，可以先收回；省略后反而更容易理解的细节，则可以继续留在游戏之外。
What Does This River Show, and What Does It Leave Out?

The animal crossing tracks positions, planks, and rounds. It does not ask us to judge wind, water depth, or whether either animal can swim. It reduces a complicated crossing to a few relationships we can understand and change. Making those choices is a way of building a model.

A model lets us think about a problem with relatively few things. Understanding it requires noticing which relationships are in the rules, which belong to pictures or stories, and which do not appear at all.
What question remains after the omissions?

In the basic game, each move costs one plank, only animals at the start can collect, and both must arrive by the end of round four. Together these relationships pose a question: who stays on the bank first so both animals have enough material and opportunities to finish? We can calculate that without knowing the water temperature.

Now suppose we draw fish in the river and introduce the game as protecting the river. If every action still changes only animal positions and the plank supply, players cannot affect the fish through their choices. The picture includes fish; the rules have yet to express how protection happens.

To make protection something players consider, we would need to choose a relationship, such as how an action affects fish, then specify its visible consequence and connection to reaching the far bank. Each addition can create more to understand and record. We could instead keep the fish as scenery and describe this version as planning a shared crossing. A model can be small. Its promises should fit what it actually expresses.
Connections also take a position
Leave the animals briefly for a completely fictional model of riverside messages. This is independent of the crossing game.

There are three households, A, B, and C, in a line. A neighbors B, and B neighbors C; A and C are not neighbors. Initially none knows a message. A player has two announcement tokens. Spending one selects a household for a reading; that household and its immediate neighbors learn the message at once. The message spreads no further, and those who know remember it. The task finishes immediately when all three know. Otherwise, it ends incomplete when both tokens are spent.

Selecting B once informs B and both neighbors, A and C, completing the task with one token. Selecting A first informs only A and B; selecting C afterward informs the remaining household, using two tokens altogether. We can calculate these results from the stated rules.

But why does a neighbor definitely hear? Why does nobody tell a friend afterward? This model makes distance a condition for transmission and makes an announcement certain to work. It leaves out trust, language, and other connections. Those choices make the middle household particularly effective. The rules express a way of considering a problem, rather than a picture of reality without any choices behind it.

Using this to discuss real communication would require finding out whether those relationships hold in reality. The fictional result establishes what happens under its stated conditions. It cannot establish that a real middle household must have the most influence.
A story can leave room that an action cannot

Return to the crossing. Why does Hedgehog stay at the bank? We can leave that without a single required answer. Someone might imagine caution; another might imagine care for a friend. If both follow the same action rules, the story has room for different interpretations.

Where collected planks go cannot remain open in the same way. In the center, both animals can use them. In a private pocket, the other animal cannot spend them directly. That changes the next available move and needs a definite rule, rather than a guess about an animal’s personality.

Rabbit and Hedgehog could have different speeds in another story, but this version gives them the same step length. That lets us attend to order and shared material. The names supply character images; equal movement is a choice made by the model.
A recollection chooses its emphasis too

Suppose somebody describes a finished game as, “Rabbit led the way and reached the bank first.” That fits our successful route but omits Hedgehog’s first collect action. “Hedgehog prepared the material so both could arrive” emphasizes support without retelling every move either.

“Rabbit discovered the route for everyone” would add a discovery absent from the rules. In the basic game, the entire route is visible from the start. Moving Rabbit reveals no new information. Stories can emphasize different things while keeping claims about an action’s consequences connected to what happened.

Write what you want players to consider beside the map, then find an action for each item. Reconsider promises that have no action to support them. Details whose omission makes the game clearer can stay outside it.
怎样让朋友照着说明就能开始？
设想朋友第一次拿到过河说明，读见“留在起点收集两块木板”，便拿了木板，又把动物向前移了一步。他可能以为收集只是移动前的准备。设计者心里知道一次只能做一件，纸上却没有让这两个动作的关系足够清楚。
写规则时，要把已经确定的玩法转成别人可以执行的说明。这包括句子，也包括他眼前的物品摆法。
先让人知道要完成什么
读者还没认识石头和木板，就先看到例外条款，很难知道它们为何重要。可以先交代：“两人合作，在最多四轮内让小兔和小刺猬都到对岸。”再说明小林控制小兔，小雨控制小刺猬，两只都从起点开始；路线依次是起点、第一块石头、第二块石头、对岸。
这给细节一个位置。前进不是随便移动，而是花中央一块木板，走到前方的相邻位置；两只可以站在同一个地方，不会堵住彼此。“前方的相邻位置”也比只写“走一步”少留一个方向疑问。
随后说明时间：“每轮小林先行动一次，小雨再行动一次，两人都行动过才结束这一轮。”一个人的回合和两个人合起来的一轮，在这里各有清楚的范围。
把误读发生的连接处写出来
动作部分可以先写：“轮到你时，只选以下一件事。”然后给出前进、收集和等待。收集写成：“只有动物还在起点时可以选择；动物留在原地，从备用纸片拿两块新木板加入中央。”等待则既不移动，也不取得木板。
这样，收集不再像免费的开场准备，它本身就是这次行动。条件和动作挨在一起，也让人不必翻到最后才发现石头上的动物不能收集。已经到对岸的动物以后只能等待，可以放在说明前进结果的附近，再收入查阅提示。
例子接着走一次就能检验句子是否接得起来。第一轮小林花一块，移动小兔，中央从四块变三块；小雨收集两块新木板，小刺猬仍在起点，中央成为五块。两人都行动过，现在才把轮数改到第二轮。例子没有给任何人一次额外移动。
结束也要落到明确时点：两只都到岸，立即获胜；否则第四轮结束时失败。不必在两只已经到齐后再补一个没有用途的行动。
桌上有三种纸片位置
中央可用木板、旁边已用木板和桌外备用纸片承担不同作用。中央的是玩家现在拥有的共享资源；花掉的移到已用区，不能再次收集回来；备用的用来表示后来取得的新木板，现在还不能拿来支付前进。
纸片基本版可以准备二十片：四片放中央，十六片备用。四轮共最多八次行动，即使每次都是收集，备用十六片也够表示。这个数量是在准备组件，不是给玩家新增一个需要争抢的有限仓库。若以后延长轮数，也要为新版本准备足够纸片。
把三处清楚隔开，比要求人记住“这些虽然堆在一起，却有些不能用”更容易查明当前局面。名称也要稳定：动作中叫木板，图里却叫桥梁、列表又叫建筑资源，就会让人怀疑是否有三种东西。
醒目的应当是现在要判断的事
一只很大的立体小兔也许很吸引人，但若挡住踏脚石，小雨就难以确认两只动物在哪。缩小它或换一种摆法，是为了让重要位置显露出来。装饰的体积和颜色会引人注意，不能只按“好不好看”决定。
轮数同样需要看得见。动物都没动，可能表示两人还没行动，也可能表示刚才都等待过，不能只从位置猜轮数。一个写着一到四的简单轮次标记，可以保存这项单看动物看不出的信息；它在两人都完成行动后更新。
第一次理解与后来查找
第一次阅读需要目标、摆法、轮流方式和一次完整动作，顺着经过理解。熟悉以后，玩家可能只想迅速找到“到了对岸还能收集吗”。简短的动作提示和明显的小标题可以帮助查找，但关键条件仍应出现在完整说明里，不能只藏在一张容易丢失的小卡上。
写完后，沿说明摆出第一轮。每读到一个名字，就在桌上找到它；每完成一个动作，就核对留下的结果。纸上的句子和桌上的东西对得上，别人接手时才少一处猜测。
How Can a Friend Begin from the Instructions?

Imagine a friend reading the crossing rules for the first time. The instruction says, “Stay at the start and collect two planks.” The friend takes the planks, then moves the animal forward. Perhaps collecting seemed like preparation before moving. The designer knows that a turn permits only one action, but the page has not made the relationship clear enough.
Writing rules means turning the settled design into instructions somebody else can execute. That includes sentences and the arrangement of the objects in front of them.
First explain what people are trying to finish

A reader encountering exceptions before the stones and planks may struggle to understand their purpose. Begin with the goal: “Work together to get Rabbit and Hedgehog across within four rounds.” Then introduce Lin controlling Rabbit, Yu controlling Hedgehog, and both starting on the near bank. The route is the start, first stone, second stone, and far bank, in that order.

Details now have a place. Moving means spending one plank from the center to reach the next adjacent position ahead. Both animals can occupy the same place without blocking each other. Naming the direction resolves a question that “move one step” could leave open.

Explain the timing too: “In each round, Lin takes one turn, then Yu takes one turn. The round ends after both have acted.” One person’s turn and the round containing both turns now have distinct scopes.
Write the connection where a misreading occurs

Start the actions with, “On your turn, choose exactly one of the following.” Then give move, collect, and wait. For collect, write: “You may choose this only while your animal is at the start. Leave it there, take two new planks from the reserve paper pieces, and add them to the center.” Waiting moves nothing and gains no planks.

Collecting now reads as the turn’s action rather than a free preliminary step. Keeping the condition beside the action also avoids making players discover much later that an animal on a stone cannot collect. Explain that an animal on the far bank can only wait on later turns near the consequences of moving, and include it in a reference reminder too.

Continue with a worked round to see whether the sentences connect. Lin spends one plank and moves Rabbit, reducing the central supply from four to three. Yu collects two new planks; Hedgehog stays at the start and the supply becomes five. Both have now acted, so the round marker advances to round two. Neither receives an extra move.

Place the ending at a definite moment: both animals arriving means an immediate win; otherwise, the end of round four means a loss. There is no need for a purposeless extra action after both have arrived.
Paper pieces belong in three different places

Available planks in the center, used planks beside them, and reserve paper pieces off the table have different roles. The center holds the shared resource the players currently own. Spent planks enter the used area and cannot be collected again. Reserve pieces represent newly obtained planks later; they cannot pay for a move now.

For the basic paper version, prepare twenty pieces: four in the center and sixteen in reserve. Four rounds allow at most eight actions, so sixteen reserve pieces suffice even if every action is collect. This prepares the components; it does not add a limited warehouse for players to compete over. A version with more rounds needs enough paper pieces for that version too.

Separating the three places makes the position easier to check than asking people to remember which pieces in a mixed pile are usable. Names should remain consistent as well. Calling the same item a plank in an action, a bridge in a picture, and a building resource in a list can make it seem like three different things.
Make the current judgment easy to see

A large Rabbit figure may attract attention, but if it hides a stepping stone, Yu may struggle to identify the animals’ positions. Reducing its size or changing its placement can reveal information that matters. Decorative size and color direct attention, so appearance is more than a question of liking the look.

The round must also remain visible. Unmoved animals could mean neither player has acted, or that both just waited. Positions alone cannot identify the round. A simple marker labeled one through four can preserve that otherwise invisible information. It updates after both players complete their actions.
Understanding first, finding a detail later

A first reading needs the goal, setup, turn order, and a complete action in an understandable sequence. Later, someone may only want to find whether an animal on the far bank can collect. Short action reminders and clear headings support that search. Essential conditions should also appear in the complete instructions, rather than only on a small card that could go missing.

Follow the instructions through the first round. Find each named object on the table and check what each action leaves behind. Matching sentences to pieces gives the next reader fewer gaps to guess across.
帮朋友时，怎样保留她的决定？
设想小雨轮到行动，却迟迟没动小刺猬。可能是中央纸片互相压住，她看不清还有几块；可能是她知道要收集，却难以捏起很薄的纸片；也可能是动作都懂，正在想这次是否该走。外表都是停下来，需要的帮助却不同。
前面选择游玩情境时，我们问过谁会在什么条件下加入。现在已经有动作和材料，就能把这个问题落实到一次具体参与：她需要看见什么、操作什么，又想自己决定什么？
先分清卡住的是哪一步
假如小雨说“我数不清”，可以把中央木板分开摆，或让她从当前位置就能看清数量。如果她说“不知道哪堆能花”，需要说明可用、已用与备用三处，而不仅是再报一次数量。
假如她说“我想收集，纸太薄拿不起来”，她已经作出了决定。可以换成较厚的片，或由别人按她的选择移动纸片。若她说“我还在想”，马上替她选收集，就解决了一个她没有提出的操作问题，同时中止了她自己的考虑。
所以帮助可以从一句具体的话开始：“你需要我说清哪里，还是帮你移动哪几片？”不是每次停顿都要打断询问，但已经要介入时，先确认需要，比从动作快慢猜原因可靠。
让同一信息有多种认法
基本版的木板数量和动物位置对两人都公开。如果两只动物只靠相近颜色区分，可以加上小兔、小刺猬的轮廓或名字；若纸片文字太小，可以放大关键名称。颜色、形状和文字相互补充，让人不必只依靠一种线索。
增加线索也要检查它们是否一致。图上小兔在第一块石头，旁边说明却写第二块，给得更多反而制造冲突。一张很长的提示纸若把棋盘推到远处，也可能让读字更方便、够到动物却更困难。
材料令人喜欢和材料容易使用，还需要分别考虑。有分量的木片可能让某人喜欢拿在手里；过大的动物也可能遮住它站的石头。不能从“看起来更精美”直接推得更容易参与。这里需要知道具体哪个物品、哪一步操作出了问题。
移动物品的人，可以不是决定的人
假设小雨的小刺猬仍在起点，她说：“我选收集，请帮我从备用拿两片放到中央。”小林照做，小刺猬不动，小雨这次行动结束。这仍是小雨选择的收集，纸片由谁捏起来没有改变动作结果。
若小林为了方便，每轮都自己替两只动物选好动作，就改变了决定归谁。小雨即使仍亲手放片，也未必保留了真正的选择。操作支持与策略建议因此可以分开：“我可以替你摆”不等于“我替你决定摆什么”。
建议也可以保留自主权。小林能说明“两只都先走会缺木板”，再让小雨想一想。前面合作章已经解释过这份理由；这里要保证获得说明后，她仍能表达自己的选择，别人也按那个选择执行。
反馈不必要求每个人表演一样
每次前进以后，看见动物到了哪块石头、中央少了一块木板，就是有用的动作反馈。如果介绍要求玩家必须站起来模仿跳跃，才算移动成功，身体表演便成为新增的参与条件。
有人可能喜欢这项表演，另一个人可能不愿在大家面前做。若设计方向仍是商量过河，可以把模仿留作自愿表达，让说出行动或指明目的地同样能完成选择。想专门设计动作表演游戏，则应重新说明玩法条件，不能把不想表演误当作不懂合作。
感到自在也不能只靠拿得到棋子保证。一个帮助动作是否被请求、别人有没有公开评价她的手法，都可能改变这次相处。我们可以提供表达需要的办法，再听实际参加者怎样描述，不能替她预先宣布“已经舒服了”。
改哪一层，结果就在哪一层变化
把片换厚、把共用木板摆近、接受口头选择，可以支持执行原来的动作。额外送小刺猬一次前进，则会改变它的行动机会，属于规则变体，需要重新计算和说明。两类改动都可以讨论，只是解决的问题不同。
把支持方式放回原来的任务里试：哪一步更容易了，决定仍由谁作出？如果代拿木板解决了操作困难，却把选择也交给了同伴，就还需要调整帮助的方法。
How Can Help Preserve Her Decision?

Imagine Yu pausing on her turn without moving Hedgehog. Overlapping paper pieces might hide the number of available planks. She might know she wants to collect but struggle to pick up thin paper. Or she might understand every action and still be deciding whether to move. The visible pause is similar; the useful help differs.

When choosing a play setting, we asked who would join and under what conditions. With actions and materials in place, we can now examine one concrete moment: what does she need to perceive and handle, and what does she want to decide herself?
Find the step that is difficult

If Yu says, “I cannot count them,” spreading the central planks apart or making their number visible from her seat may help. If she says, “I do not know which pile I can spend,” explain the available, used, and reserve areas. Repeating the number alone would not answer that question.

If she says, “I want to collect, but the paper is too thin to pick up,” she has already decided. Thicker pieces could help, or somebody could move them according to her choice. If she says, “I am still thinking,” choosing collect for her would address a handling problem she never reported while ending her consideration.

Help can therefore begin with a concrete offer: “Would you like something explained, or help moving some pieces?” Every pause need not prompt an interruption. When intervening, however, checking the need is more reliable than inferring it from speed alone.
Give the same information more than one recognizable form

In the basic game, plank counts and animal positions are public to both people. If similar colors alone distinguish the animals, add Rabbit and Hedgehog shapes or names. If the words on pieces are too small, enlarge the essential labels. Color, shape, and wording can complement one another so a person need not depend on just one cue.

Additional cues must agree. Showing Rabbit on the first stone while a nearby description says the second creates a conflict. A long reference sheet that pushes the board away may make reading easier while making the animal harder to reach.

Appealing materials and usable materials also deserve separate attention. Someone might enjoy the weight of a wooden piece. A large animal figure might hide its stone. Looking more elaborate does not establish that participation becomes easier. We need to identify the particular object and action involved.
The person moving a piece need not make the decision

Suppose Hedgehog is still at the start and Yu says, “I choose collect. Please take two reserve pieces and put them in the center for me.” Lin does so, Hedgehog stays still, and Yu’s turn ends. It remains her chosen collect action. Which fingers moved the paper does not change its result.

If Lin conveniently chooses both animals’ actions every round, he changes who decides. Yu might still place pieces herself while having little choice left. Handling assistance and strategic advice can therefore be separate: offering to place something does not give permission to decide what to place.

Advice can preserve agency too. Lin can explain why both animals moving first would leave them short of planks, then let Yu consider it. The cooperation chapter developed that reason. Here we need to ensure that she can express her choice afterward and that any assistance follows it.
Feedback need not require the same performance from everyone

After a move, seeing the animal on its new stone and one fewer available plank provides useful feedback. Requiring the player to stand up and imitate a jump before that move counts would add a bodily performance as a condition of participation.

One person might enjoy performing while another would rather not do it in front of the group. If the design still aims at discussing a shared crossing, imitation can remain optional, with speaking an action or indicating a destination also allowing a choice. A game specifically about performing movements would need its conditions explained afresh. Reluctance to perform cannot simply be treated as failure to understand cooperation.

Being able to reach a piece does not guarantee feeling comfortable either. Whether help was requested, or whether others publicly judge her handling, can affect the encounter. We can provide ways to express a need and listen to participants’ actual accounts without announcing in advance that someone now feels at ease.
The kind of change determines what it changes

Thicker pieces, a closer shared supply, and spoken choices can support the existing actions. Giving Hedgehog an extra move changes its opportunities and creates a rule variation that needs fresh calculation and explanation. Both kinds of change are open to discussion; they address different problems.
Try the support in the original task. Which step became easier, and who still makes the decision? If helping someone handle planks also hands their choice to a companion, adjust the help.
这一轮，原型要做得多准确？
早在写动作时，我们就已经能拿纸片玩过河了。现在读过更多规则与呈现方式，桌上的问题也变多了：两人有没有时间到岸？可用和已用木板会不会混淆？坐在桌子另一边能否读清动作提示？这些问题都可以用草稿来查，却不需要把每个地方做到同样精细。
这种让设计可以被实际操作和检查的草稿，就是原型。它的精度，指它在我们关心的地方和准备做出的玩法有多接近。精度不是整件作品从“粗糙”到“精美”的单一排名。一张没有装饰的纸，可以把动作顺序表示得很准确；一张漂亮图片，也可能根本不能运行一局。
先问，这次必须保留什么？
若想知道四轮里能否完成基本版过河，纸上写数字、移动两只动物就够开始检查。位置、每步花一块、只在起点收集两块、每人每轮一次和四轮期限必须准确。动物的毛色不影响这次核算。
如果这次要看新玩家怎样区分木板，精度要求就换了。二十张纸片中，四张可用、十六张备用，旁边还要有已用区；这些区的名称、距离和拿取方式正是被检查的内容。我们不能一边替玩家把所有纸片放好，一边说材料已经能够自行说明去向。
再换一个问题：对面的人看不看得清“只能在起点收集”？把文字放大到整页、拿到他眼前，当然可能让他读清，却没有检查实际桌面上的提示。此时应保留准备使用的字大小、摆放位置和观看距离。其他不相关的装饰仍可以简略。
局部草稿，能回答多大的问题？
有时只需要检查开头的一小段。把两只动物摆在起点、中央放四块，演示一次前进和一次收集，就能检查这两种操作有没有漏写木板去向。这个片段还没有显示后面的选择，也没有经历第四轮，不能据此判断整局难度或重复游玩的兴趣。
如果要看两人怎样提前安排谁留下，就需要从起点玩到结束，让准备与期限真正起作用。直接给出已经快成功的局面，会把最需要观察的早期决定跳过去。原型要完整到什么程度，取决于这次问题横跨多长的过程。
局部检查也能暴露明确错误。例如收集说明没有写“新木板”，这就是值得补清的文字；不必为了证明存在这个缺口，先组织十场完整游戏。但补清以后有没有帮助别人读懂，仍要在使用新材料时观察。
材料的差别什么时候会改变结果？
基本版没有秘密信息，木板背面画得不一样，通常不影响知道中央有几块。先前讨论的天气局面却不同：若抽出的天气本该暂时保密，薄纸让人透过背面看出“下雨”，就把未知的结果提前泄露了。这时不透光的背面是让该局面正常运行的条件，不是装饰要求。天气仍只是另一个比较用的局面，不加入基本版。
同样，若想知道纸片是否容易拿起，就要实际用接近预定大小和厚度的纸片；把动作改成口头报数，会绕开手部操作。若以后做电子版，程序立即更新资源，也可能和人逐个搬动纸片时产生不同节奏。纸上核对规则有帮助，却不能凭它断言电子操作的感觉一样。
在原型旁留一句：“我想看这个人，用这些材料，能否完成这件事。”把会影响答案的部分做好，就可以先停手。等一次实际尝试告诉你缺什么，再补下一处。
How Accurate Does This Prototype Need to Be?

We could already play the crossing game with paper pieces when we first wrote its actions. After examining more rules and ways of presenting them, we have more questions. Can both animals arrive in time? Might available and spent planks get confused? Can someone across the table read the action reminder? Drafts can help investigate all these questions, but their parts do not need equal attention.

A draft that lets people operate and examine a design is a prototype. Its fidelity is how closely it represents the intended play in the parts we care about. Fidelity is not a single ranking from rough to beautiful. An undecorated sheet can represent action order accurately; an attractive picture might be unable to run a game at all.
What must this version preserve?

To check whether the base crossing can be completed in four rounds, we can start with written numbers and two moving animal pieces. Positions, a cost of one plank per move, collecting two only on the starting bank, one turn per player per round, and the four-round deadline must be accurate. Fur color does not affect this calculation.

To see how new players distinguish the planks, we need different details. Of twenty pieces, four are available and sixteen are spare, with another area for spent planks. The areas’ names, spacing, and handling are now part of what we are examining. If we arrange every piece for the players, we cannot also claim the materials explained the destinations on their own.

Now suppose the question is whether someone across the table can read “Collect only on the starting bank.” Enlarging the sentence to fill a page and holding it close might make it readable, but would not check the intended table reminder. We need the intended text size, position, and viewing distance. Unrelated decoration can still remain simple.
How much can a partial draft tell us?

Sometimes we need only a short section. Put both animals on the starting bank with four available planks, then demonstrate one move and one collect action. This can reveal whether the instructions omit a plank’s destination. It does not show later choices or reach the deadline, so it cannot establish the whole game’s difficulty or appeal across repeated plays.

To examine how people plan who stays behind, we need the journey from setup to ending, allowing preparation and the deadline to matter. Starting from a nearly successful position would skip the early decision we most need to observe. How complete a prototype must be depends on how much of the process the question covers.

A partial check can still expose a definite omission. If collecting never specifies that the planks are new, the wording needs clarification. We need not organize ten complete games to establish that a sentence is missing. Whether the revised wording helps another person understand still requires observing its use.
When do material differences change the result?

The base game has no secret information. Different marks on the backs of planks usually do not change our knowledge of the shared total. The earlier weather example is different. If a drawn card should remain secret but thin paper reveals “Rain” through its back, an unknown result has been disclosed early. An opaque back is then necessary for that situation to work, rather than an ornamental detail. Weather remains a separate comparison and is not added to the base game.

Likewise, to examine whether pieces are easy to pick up, use pieces close to the intended size and thickness. Replacing movement with spoken numbers would bypass the physical action. A future digital version that updates resources instantly might also have a different pace from moving each paper piece by hand. Checking rules on paper is useful without proving that digital interaction will feel the same.

Leave a sentence beside the prototype: “I want to see whether this person can do this task with these materials.” Make the parts that affect the answer, then stop building for now. Let an actual attempt show what needs attention next.
请朋友试玩前，要先安排什么？
把过河草稿放到朋友面前，说一句“帮我看看好不好玩”，很容易收到一句同样宽泛的回答：“还可以。”即使朋友认真玩了，设计者也可能不知道这句话指的是动物可爱、动作清楚，还是一起讨论时很开心。
一次试玩不必回答所有问题。假设我们这轮最想知道：第一次接触的人，能否分清备用、可用和已用木板，并正确完成收集？那么，请什么人、给什么材料、开头说什么，都应围绕这个问题安排。
谁来玩，会影响这次能看到什么？
熟悉上一版的朋友可以比较改动后的感觉，却已经知道收集拿的是新木板。他不再询问，不能直接证明新说明讲清了这一点。第一次接触这款游戏的人，更适合帮助检查第一次阅读会遇到什么。
“第一次接触”也不等于人人一样。一位常玩桌游的朋友，可能会主动寻找动作提示；另一位可能需要更多时间读完一段文字。如果我们想做给短暂空闲里一起玩的两名新手，就应尽量接近这种人数、经验和使用场景。只找特别擅长解释规则的人，容易漏掉材料给其他人带来的困难。
邀请时可以说明这是尚在修改的纸片游戏，想了解材料哪里需要改进；不要求对方证明自己会玩。也应说清预计占用的时间，以及可以求助、暂停或结束。愿意参加的人，才会坐下来；试玩不是获得朋友帮助的一项强制任务。
准备哪一版，怎样开始？
先把同一版材料放齐：完整基本规则、四个位置的地图、两只动物、二十张木板、轮次与回合提示，以及备用、可用、已用三个放置区。中央从四块开始，其余十六块备用，已用区为空。不要把尚未决定的天气或捷径夹进这次基本版。
为便于追踪，可以把这份待检草稿称为 v0.2。这个名字只是在区分材料，不表示它已经通过测试。说明、地图和动作提示应当对应同一版；否则一个地方写“取新木板”，另一个地方写“拿回木板”，玩家面对的是互相矛盾的材料。
如果问题是“材料能否独立讲清”，开头就先让参与者按材料准备和阅读，设计者不用抢先讲出木板答案。可以说：“我想看看这些说明是否够清楚。卡住时可以问我，想停也可以。”如果问题换成“懂规则后怎样分配收集”，则先教会规则，再观察计划更合适。主持方式应服务这次问题。
在场的人怎样帮助，又留下什么？
设计者可以留意纸片被从哪里拿走、放到哪里，以及发生了什么疑问。短记录至少应能让以后的人认出版本、当时的局面、具体动作和原话。记录“中央三块时，小雨指着已用区询问能否取回”，就比“她玩错了”更容易继续分析。
她若请求帮助，就可以解释。把解释的时刻和内容也留下，之后便知道哪些过程依靠了帮助。为看后半局而临时换一条规则也可以成为另一种探索，但应先让参与者知道，并标明从哪里开始用了改动。不能把前后两个版本当成一次完全相同的测试。
参与者不愿继续、材料缺失，或某处规则让局面无法往下走，都可以结束这次尝试。一次没有玩到第四轮的试玩仍可能暴露准备上的问题；硬撑到结束反而会把设计者的临时补充误当成原稿的能力。
试玩结束后，先找一个能带回草稿的问题。即使只发现“玩家不知道木板从哪里拿”，也已经有了一处可以核对、修改和再试的地方。
What Should You Arrange Before Inviting Friends to Playtest?

Putting the crossing draft in front of friends and asking “Is it fun?” may produce an equally broad answer: “It’s okay.” Even if they play carefully, you may not know whether they mean the animals are appealing, the actions are clear, or discussing plans was enjoyable.

A playtest does not have to answer everything. Suppose our question this time is: can first-time players distinguish spare, available, and spent planks and collect correctly? Who joins, which materials they receive, and what we say at the start should all help us examine that question.
Who plays affects what we can learn

A friend who knows the previous draft can compare how changes feel, but already knows that collecting produces new planks. Their lack of questions cannot by itself show that the new explanation is clear. Someone encountering this game for the first time is better placed to reveal difficulties with a first reading.

First-time players are not all alike either. A frequent tabletop player may look for an action reminder immediately; someone else may need longer to read a paragraph. If our intended setting is two beginners playing during a short break, we should try to approach those conditions of group size, experience, and use. Inviting only people who are especially skilled at explaining rules can hide difficulties other readers face.

Explain that this is a paper game still being revised, and that you want to find places where its materials need improvement. Participants do not need to prove they are good players. Tell them roughly how long the session is expected to take and that they may ask for help, pause, or stop. Joining should be their choice, not an obligation to help a friend.
Which version will they receive, and how will it begin?

Gather one consistent set: complete base rules, the four-space map, two animals, twenty planks, round and turn reminders, and separate areas for spare, available, and spent pieces. Start with four available planks, sixteen spare pieces, and an empty spent area. Leave undecided weather and shortcut ideas out of this base version.

We can call this draft v0.2 to distinguish its materials. The number does not mean it has passed a test. Rules, map, and action reminder must agree. If one says “take new planks” while another says “take planks back,” participants receive contradictory instructions.

If we want to know whether the materials explain themselves, let participants prepare and read from them before giving the answer about planks. An opening could be: “I want to see whether these instructions are clear enough. You can ask me if you get stuck, and you can stop whenever you want.” If the question is instead how informed players divide collecting, teaching the rules first makes more sense. The way we host should fit the question.
How can the host help and keep a useful record?

Watch where pieces are taken from and placed, and which questions arise. A short note should let someone later identify the version, situation, specific action, and words spoken. “With three available planks, Yu pointed at the spent area and asked whether she could take one back” is easier to investigate than “She played incorrectly.”

If she asks for help, explain. Record when the explanation happened and what it supplied, so later events can be understood in light of that help. Trying a temporary rule change to explore the rest of the game can also be useful, provided participants know the plan and the point of change is marked. The two versions should not be treated as one unchanged test.

Participants may want to stop. Materials may be missing, or a rule may leave no way to continue. Any of these can end the attempt. A session that never reaches round 4 can still reveal a preparation problem. Forcing it to finish can make the designer’s improvised additions look like abilities the original draft already had.
After the test, find one question you can take back to the draft. Even “the player did not know where to take planks from” gives you somewhere to check, revise, and try again.
朋友停下来时，我们究竟知道了什么？
上一章安排了一个具体问题：第一次接触过河游戏的人，能否分清备用、可用和已用木板？下面用一段为讲解编写的假想试玩，看看现场记录怎样帮助判断。这里的 v0.2 是待检草稿的名字，人物动作和对话都不是已经发生的测试。
这一稿使用基本规则：中央先有四块可用木板，另有十六块备用；前进一步花一块，花过的不再使用；动物仍在起点时，可以用一个回合收集两块新木板。草稿有完整规则，但桌上三处放置区的区别还需要检查。
把一小段事件留下来
设想第一轮小林让小兔前进，花一块木板放入已用区。中央剩三块。轮到小雨，她的小刺猬还在起点。她拿起刚花过的木板，指向中央，问：“收集是不是拿回已经用过的木板？”
这段记录留下了位置、数量、动作和一句询问。我们知道她正在确认收集的来源。她还没有完成收集，也不能凭她拿起纸片就说她选择了哪一种完整玩法。
“小雨没认真读规则”却不是同样性质的记录。它已经替动作指定了一个原因。她可能漏看了“新木板”，可能没把备用纸片和规则中的新木板联系起来，也可能熟悉另一款会回收资源的游戏。即使完整规则写着正确答案，桌面提示仍可能把注意力引向别处。
玩家解释能补充什么？
主持者可以先问：“你刚才觉得收集的木板应该从哪里来？”这个问题让小雨描述自己的理解，而不是要求她认同某个原因。若直接问“是不是这几堆摆得太近？”，她听到的已经包含一个现成答案。
继续这个假想片段。小雨回答：“我以为旁边那堆就是要重新拿的。”这句话支持一个较窄的判断：她当时把已用区当成了收集来源。它还没有区分，是摆放位置、文字，还是她先前的经验促成了这种理解。
动作和解释可以互相补充，却不能让设计者读到别人所有想法。她说自己以为能取回，不等于所有新玩家都会这样想；一次询问也不能证明整款游戏太难。保留这个范围，下一步才知道还要查什么。
帮助发生后，结论要跟着改变
假设主持者随后解释：“收集拿两块新木板，从备用区取。花过的木板不会回来。”小雨于是从备用区拿两块放到中央，可用数量从三变五，小刺猬仍在起点，回合结束。
现在可以记下：听过解释后，她完成了这次收集。不能把后面的正确操作算成原材料独立讲清的证明。帮助并没有毁掉整场试玩，它只是改变了我们可以用这段过程回答的问题。
同样，如果主持者在她拿起纸片前就说“别拿那堆”，原本可能发生的询问便看不到了。若这次要检查首次理解，提前提醒会遮住要看的部分；若这次要观察懂规则后的合作，先解释反而可能合适。记录版本之外，也要记住现场多了哪些话。
暂时把改法留在问题后面
给三个区加明显名称，或者把收集写成“从备用区取两块”，都是可以考虑的做法。但这段记录本身还没有比较这些改法，更没有证明其中一个已经有效。
此刻我们可以把结论写得具体一点：“在这段假想片段里，小雨询问能否回收已用木板；解释来源后，她正确收集。接下来需要查材料哪里让收集来源不清楚。”这比“玩家不懂”更能指导下一步，也没有把猜测伪装成事实。
整理其他记录时，也保留这样的动作与原话。有人说木板不够，有人想多一轮，有人误读收集；把他们所处的局面放在一起，才能知道这些反馈是否需要同一种改法。
What Do We Know When a Friend Stops to Ask?

The previous chapter set a specific question: can someone new to the crossing game distinguish spare, available, and spent planks? We will use an invented playtest scene to examine how a record can support a judgment. Here, v0.2 names a draft awaiting examination. The actions and dialogue are examples, not results of a test that has taken place.

This draft uses the base rules: four available planks and sixteen spare pieces at setup; one plank spent per move, never reused; and an animal on the starting bank may use a turn to collect two new planks. The draft includes complete rules, but we still need to examine how clearly its three areas communicate their different roles.
Preserve a small sequence of events

Imagine that Lin moves Rabbit in round 1 and puts one plank in the spent area. Three planks remain available. It is Yu’s turn, and Hedgehog is still on the starting bank. She picks up the plank Lin just spent, points toward the center, and asks, “Does collecting mean taking back planks that have already been used?”

This account preserves positions, a quantity, an action, and a question. We know she is checking where collected planks come from. She has not yet completed a collect action. Picking up a piece alone does not establish which complete procedure she intends to follow.

“Yu did not read carefully” is a different kind of statement. It has already assigned a cause. She may have missed “new planks,” failed to connect the spare pieces with that phrase, or remembered another game in which resources return. Even if the complete rules contain the correct answer, the table layout could still direct attention elsewhere.
What can the player’s explanation add?

The host could ask, “Where did you think the collected planks should come from?” This invites Yu to describe her understanding. “Are those piles too close together?” supplies a possible explanation before she answers.

Continue the imagined scene. Yu says, “I thought that pile beside us was the one we were supposed to take from again.” This supports a narrower judgment: at that moment, she treated the spent area as the source for collecting. It does not yet establish whether placement, wording, or previous experience led her there.

Actions and explanations can inform each other without revealing every thought. Her expectation that pieces return does not mean every new player will expect the same. One question cannot establish that the whole game is too difficult. Keeping the claim within these limits shows us what still needs investigation.
Help changes what the next event can show

Suppose the host explains: “Collecting gives you two new planks from the spare area. Spent planks do not return.” Yu then takes two spare pieces and adds them to the center. The available supply rises from three to five, Hedgehog stays on the starting bank, and her turn ends.

We can now record that she completed this collect action after an explanation. We cannot count that correct action as proof that the original materials explained themselves. Helping has not ruined the entire session; it has changed which questions this part can answer.

Likewise, if the host says “Don’t take from that pile” before Yu reaches for it, we cannot see the question that might otherwise have emerged. For a first-understanding check, an early reminder can hide the very thing we want to examine. For a session about cooperation after learning the rules, explaining first may be appropriate. Alongside the version, keep track of words added during the session.
Keep proposed fixes after the question
Prominent labels for the three areas, or an instruction saying “Take two from the spare area,” are possible changes. This record has not compared them or established that either works.

For now, a precise conclusion is: “In this imagined scene, Yu asked whether spent planks could be collected. After the source was explained, she collected correctly. Next we need to investigate which part of the materials leaves that source unclear.” This gives us a better next step than “The player doesn’t understand,” while keeping guesses separate from events.

Keep actions and original remarks when sorting the other records too. Too few planks, a wish for another round, and a misread collection rule may need different revisions. Put their positions alongside one another before grouping the feedback.
听到几种说法，先查哪件事？
“木板不够。”“再多一轮就好了。”“收集是拿回用过的木板吗？”如果试玩后留下这三句话，下一稿是不是应该同时增加木板、延长游戏，再重写说明？先别急。三句话听起来都和过河困难有关，背后的事情却可能不同。
上一章跟过一次观察，现在把几份记录放到一起。本章的三桌试玩都是假设，用来示范怎样判断，没有实际发生过。它们使用同一份基本版规则和说明，暂叫 v0.2：两只动物各向前走三个相邻位置，不能退回或跳格，共用四块木板；前进一步花一块，只有起点能收集两块新木板；每轮小林先、小雨后，各行动一次，最多四轮，两只都到岸立即成功。等待也是一次行动。这里没有天气、捷径或个人分数。
先把话放回发生的地方
第一桌的记录写着：第一轮小林前进，小雨也前进。两只都站在第一块石头，中央剩两块木板。随后有人说：“木板不够。”
这个局面确实无法完成。每只还要走两步，一共需要四块；只有两块，而且已经没有动物留在起点收集。但这不能证明开局四块必定不够：第一章那条成功路线中，有一只先留下收集。我们知道的是这次出发安排用尽了补充机会。玩家是否早已理解这个后果、发现后是否觉得有意思，还没有记录。
第二桌不同。前两轮，小林都收集，小雨都前进。现在小兔仍在起点，小刺猬在第二块石头，中央有六块木板：四块加上两次收集的四块，再减去两次前进的两块。有人说：“再多一轮就好了。”
这里木板有余，小兔却只剩两次行动，来不及走三步。加木板解决不了这次困难；多给一轮确实能让它多走一步。不过，“这一条走法能完成”和“我们想把整局改长”是两个不同判断。新期限也会改变其他走法，还要回到作品希望给人的思考空间再决定。
第三桌在第一轮首次收集前问：“收集是拿回用过的木板吗？”主持者解释要从桌外备用纸片拿两块新木板，此后他们才继续。这份记录首先指向说明怎样被理解。提示后的顺畅，不能算作原说明已经让人独立理解。
相似的抱怨，不一定是同一个问题
若把三桌都归到“过河太难”，下一稿就可能只剩降低难度这一种方向。回到过程，我们却找到了三种待查的事情：出发前有没有看见补充机会，准备时有没有同时看剩余回合，以及收集动作本身有没有说清。
也不要反过来立刻写成“三个原因已查明”。我们能算出前两桌为什么走不完，却还不知道他们为什么选了那条路。或许没注意期限，或许想试试极端办法，也可能只是没有把两人的计划放在一起。第三桌提出了疑问，也不证明每位初读者都会这样理解。
一个有用的问题可以很具体：“第一桌决定让两只都离岸前，有没有讨论以后从哪里拿木板？”如果原记录没有这一段，就写“没记录到”。下一次可以观察这段商量，或在局后请玩家回想当时打算怎么继续。回想也是当事人的说明，不能当作当时逐字发生的对话。
这样整理之后，一张意见纸不再只是待执行的点子清单。每句话都有一个发生位置、一份目前支持它的记录，以及仍不知道的部分。
再确认，我们比较的是不是同一份东西
假如第四份记录来自五轮版，把它与四轮版的成功失败混在一起，就会丢掉最关键的差别。若有人已经玩过三次，有人第一次见图，他们对准备阶段的理解也未必相同。版本、参与经验、初始局面和主持给过的帮助，都应当跟着记录留下。
这不表示这些记录不能相互启发。五轮版可能让我们看见一种四轮里来不及发展的计划；回访的朋友可能发现原来漏掉的配合。只是两者不能被压成一个“不管怎么改都有人输”的总数字。
如果主持中途让大家试了新规则，可以在记录上划出改变发生的位置，分别写出前后的规则。它能帮助探索新办法，但那场试玩不再是从头到尾检验同一版本。把差别标出来，后来的自己或合作者才知道哪一段回答了哪个问题。
先处理哪项，取决于这轮想弄清什么
假设这轮的目标是“让第一次看到材料的人理解怎样收集”，第三桌的问题就很直接，值得先查说明与纸片分区。即使只有一个人问过，也可能让一次基本动作无法继续。不能因为另外两句都提到过河困难，就简单以二比一决定先延长游戏。
如果这轮已确认参加者都懂收集，而目的是观察两个人怎样商量出发，那么前两桌更值得回看。可以先看他们何时注意到补充与期限，暂时保留四轮规则。发现合法但无法完成的计划，是这个玩法的一部分；设计者要进一步判断，它是否为想邀请的人留下了可理解、值得再试的学习机会。
还有些意见需要先澄清才好排序。例如“太复杂”可能指一句规则，也可能指每次都要算很多步。先请人指出一处具体时刻，比把整部游戏判为复杂更能帮助下一稿。
把诊断交给下一次决定
这次整理可以留下这样一段暂定判断：“v0.2 的两条走法分别卡在补充机会和行动次数，尚不能说明所有开局都无法成功；另有一次对收集来源的疑问，经解释后继续。先检查说明能否让初读者分清备用、可用和已用木板，再观察他们怎样规划出发。”
留下这段改稿说明，再把原记录附在旁边。别人就能跟着看，你为什么先改这一处；下次反馈回来，也有依据判断要不要继续。
Several Comments, One Next Question

“There aren’t enough planks.” “One more round would fix it.” “Does collecting mean taking back used planks?” If these three comments follow a playtest, should the next draft add planks, extend the game, and rewrite the instructions all at once? First, look closer. All three sound like trouble crossing the river, but they may concern different events.

The previous chapter followed one observation. Now we will bring several records together. All three sessions in this chapter are hypothetical examples, not tests that actually happened. They use the same basic rules and instructions, which we will call v0.2: each animal needs three moves to cross, moving only to the next position ahead without going backward or skipping a position; the players share four planks; moving one step costs one plank; collecting two new planks is possible only on the starting bank. Each round gives Lin one turn, then Yu one turn. There are at most four rounds, and both animals arriving ends the game immediately with a shared win. Waiting also uses a turn. There is no weather, shortcut, or personal score here.
Put Each Comment Back Where It Happened
The first record says that Lin moved in the first round, then Yu moved too. Both animals stood on the first stone, with two shared planks left. Someone then said, “There aren’t enough planks.”

That position really cannot lead to success. Each animal needs two more moves, costing four planks in total. Only two remain, and neither animal is still on the starting bank to collect. But this does not show that starting with four planks always makes success impossible: in the successful sequence from chapter one, one animal stayed behind to collect. What we know is that this departure plan used up the opportunity to replenish the supply. The record does not tell us whether the players understood that consequence beforehand or found the discovery interesting.

The second table took a different route. In each of the first two rounds, Lin collected while Yu moved. Rabbit is still on the starting bank; Hedgehog is on the second stone. Six planks remain: the initial four, plus four from two collections, minus two spent moving. Someone says, “One more round would fix it.”

Here the shared supply is sufficient, but Rabbit has only two turns left to make three moves. Adding planks cannot fix that difficulty. An extra round would indeed allow another move. Yet making this particular plan succeed is a different decision from extending the whole game. A new deadline would affect other plans too. We still need to consider the thinking space we want the game to offer.

At the third table, before the first collect action in round one, someone asks, “Does collecting mean taking back used planks?” The facilitator explains that collecting takes two new planks from the spare paper pieces outside the playing area. Play then continues. This record first points to how the instructions were understood. Play going smoothly after a prompt does not show that the original instructions worked independently.
Similar Complaints May Describe Different Problems

If we group all three records under “Crossing is too difficult,” lowering the difficulty may seem like the only response. Following the events reveals three things to investigate: whether the players noticed their opportunity to collect before departing, whether preparation included checking remaining turns, and whether collecting itself was clear.

Do not jump to the opposite conclusion that three causes have now been established. We can calculate why the first two plans fail, but we do not yet know why those players chose them. They may have overlooked the deadline, wanted to try an extreme approach, or failed to consider both animals’ plans together. The third table asked a question; that does not establish that every first-time reader would interpret the rule in the same way.

A useful question can be quite specific: “Before sending both animals off the bank, did the first table discuss where later planks would come from?” If that part is missing from the record, write that it was not recorded. Next time, we could observe that discussion or ask afterward how the players had planned to continue. A recollection is still the player’s account, not a word-for-word record of the conversation at the time.
Organized this way, a page of comments becomes more than a list of changes to make. Each comment has a place in the game, a record that currently supports it, and something still unknown.
Check Whether the Records Concern the Same Thing

Suppose a fourth record comes from a five-round version. Combining its wins and losses with those from the four-round version would discard a crucial difference. Someone playing for the fourth time may also understand preparation differently from someone seeing the board for the first time. Keep the version, prior experience, starting position, and any help from the facilitator with each record.

These records can still inform one another. Five rounds might reveal a plan that has no time to develop in four. A returning friend might discover a way to cooperate that everyone previously missed. They should not, however, be compressed into a single total saying, “People lose whatever we change.”

If the facilitator introduces a new rule during play, mark where the change happened and record the rules before and after it. That session can help explore an idea, but it no longer checks one unchanged version from beginning to end. Keeping the distinction lets a future collaborator—or your future self—see which part answers which question.
What Comes First Depends on This Round of Investigation

Suppose the purpose is to find out whether people seeing the materials for the first time understand collecting. The third table raises a direct question about the instructions and the areas for paper pieces. Even a question asked by one person can prevent a basic action from continuing. Two other comments about crossing do not create a two-to-one vote for extending the game instead.

If we have already established that the participants understand collecting, and want to observe how they discuss departure, the first two tables deserve closer attention. We could examine when they noticed the need for more planks and the deadline, while keeping the four-round rule for now. Discovering a legal plan that cannot succeed is part of this game. The designer must then consider whether that discovery offers the intended players an understandable reason to try again.

Some comments need clarification before we can prioritize them. “Too complicated” might describe one sentence or the need to calculate many moves every turn. Asking for a particular moment helps the next draft more than labeling the entire game complicated.
Carry the Diagnosis into the Next Decision

This review could leave a provisional conclusion like this: “In v0.2, two plans ran into different limits: the opportunity to replenish planks and the number of turns left. These records do not show that every opening must fail. Another player asked where collected planks came from and continued after an explanation. First check whether the instructions distinguish spare, available, and spent planks for a new reader, then observe how players plan their departure.”
Keep the revision note beside the original record. Someone else can follow why this change comes first, and the next feedback will have a decision to be compared against.
下一稿，先改哪里？
上一章把三份假想记录分开看了：双方第一轮都前进，后来发现木板不够；小林连续两轮收集，后来发现小兔来不及；还有一次初读，把收集理解成拿回已用木板。这些都来自讲解用的假想 v0.2，并不是已经完成的真人测试。
现在桌上出现三个建议：多给木板、多给一轮、把收集来源写清。我们需要决定下一稿先做什么。最响亮的建议、最容易实施的改动，或者最有趣的新点子，都不能独自替我们作决定。先回到这一轮希望解决的问题。
让改动对准目前的目标
如果当前目标是“让初次接触的人正确运行基本版，再观察他们怎样共同安排”，收集来源不清会妨碍后面的判断。玩家若把已用木板拿回来，玩到的是另一套资源规则；我们便不能从后续成败判断基本版的安排是否容易理解。
因此，可以先做一个材料版本 v0.3：在桌面上清楚区分“备用纸片”“可用木板”“已用木板”，把收集写成“从备用区取两块新木板放入中央”，并在前进处写明花掉的木板不再使用。这几处需要配合改变，因为玩家会同时看地图和动作提示。它们一起澄清同一个关系，收集数量、移动代价和四轮期限都不改。
这是一项有理由的优先选择，还不是新材料已经有效的结论。下一次需要看第一次接触的人如何使用它。原来的参与者如果已经听过解释，可以比较新旧材料，却无法重新提供一次完全陌生的初读。
同一个抱怨，可以对应不同改法
“木板不够”可以是真的：双方第一轮都前进后，中央剩两块，而两只动物还共需四步。直接把初始木板从四块改成六块，会让双方一直前进也能到岸，收集便不再是完成过河所必需的准备。这个版本可能值得另试，但它改变了我们希望玩家商量的内容，不能代替澄清木板去向。
“再多一轮”也确实能救某些安排。同一只动物连续收集两次，剩余两轮只能走两步，基本版却需要三步；第五轮会给它多一次前进机会。然而，“有机会完成”和“多一轮更有趣”是两个结论。前者可以核算，后者还涉及人如何感受等待和规划。
把玩家提出的改法放回他遇到的处境里，能同时尊重问题和检查方案。我们不需要因为暂时不加一轮，就否认他确实遇到了时间不足。
确定的错误，与想探索的方向
有些事情不必靠投票判断。若我们把期限误写成三轮，双方总共只有六个回合，而到岸已经需要六次前进；最初只有四块木板，又至少需要一次收集。这些动作塞不进六个回合，基本版就不可能成功。修正这种矛盾，可以直接依据规则计算。
另一些事情是方向选择。天气会增加要应对的未知，捷径会增加路线比较，先到岸的个人奖励会把共同过河和个人竞争放在一起。它们各有可能，但都比“玩家是否理解收集来源”多出新的问题。先把它们留作单独版本，能让当前改稿保持清楚的目的。
也不必永远只做最小修改。如果多条规则一起造成了我们不想要的玩法，可能需要重新设计整段过程。此时要写清一起改了哪些关系，以及为什么。少改的价值在于更容易理解变化，不能变成拒绝解决问题的理由。
这一稿先统一木板去向的文字和摆放；额外木板、轮数和新机制分别留档。把同一版材料放成一套，再请没见过它的人从准备开始，看看还有哪些说明需要你补充。
What Should the Next Draft Change First?

The previous chapter separated three hypothetical records: both animals moved in round 1 and later lacked planks; Lin collected in two consecutive rounds and left Rabbit too little time; and one first reading treated collecting as taking back spent planks. These are teaching examples for an imagined v0.2, not completed tests with real players.

We now have three suggestions: add planks, add a round, or clarify where collected planks come from. Which should the next draft address first? The loudest suggestion, easiest change, or most exciting idea cannot decide on its own. Start with the question this round is meant to resolve.
Connect the change to the current goal

Suppose the goal is “help first-time players run the base game correctly, then observe how they plan together.” An unclear source for collected planks interferes with that later observation. If players return spent planks, they are using a different resource system. Their later success or failure cannot tell us how understandable the base game’s planning is.

We can therefore make a materials version, v0.3. Clearly separate “Spare pieces,” “Available planks,” and “Spent planks” on the table. Write collecting as “Take two new planks from the spare area and add them to the center.” State with movement that spent planks cannot be reused. These changes belong together because players consult both the map and the action reminder. They clarify one relationship while leaving collection quantity, movement cost, and the four-round deadline unchanged.

That is a reasoned priority, not a finding that the revised materials already work. We still need to observe their use by first-time players. Previous participants can compare materials, but after hearing an explanation they cannot provide another entirely unfamiliar first reading.
One complaint can lead to different changes

“There aren’t enough planks” can be accurate. After both animals move in round 1, two planks remain while four moves are still needed. Raising the starting supply from four to six would let both animals move every round and arrive without collecting. That version might be worth trying, but it changes what players need to discuss. It does not replace clarifying where planks go.

“Give us another round” can also rescue some plans. An animal that collects twice has only two turns left for movement, but needs three moves to cross. A fifth round gives it another opportunity to move. Yet “completion becomes possible” and “the extra round is more enjoyable” are different conclusions. We can calculate the first; the second involves how people experience waiting and planning.

Connecting a proposed fix to the situation that prompted it lets us take the problem seriously while examining the solution. Deferring an extra round does not deny that the player encountered a shortage of time.
Separate definite errors from directions to explore

Some questions do not need a vote. If we accidentally set a three-round deadline, both players together have only six turns. Reaching the far bank already requires six moves, while the starting four planks require at least one additional collect action. Those actions cannot fit into six turns, making success impossible. We can correct that contradiction through the rules themselves.

Other proposals change direction. Weather adds uncertainty to respond to. A shortcut adds route comparisons. A personal reward for arriving first combines a shared crossing with individual competition. Each might have value, but each introduces questions beyond whether players understand collecting. Keeping them in separate proposed versions preserves the purpose of the current revision.

We do not always need the smallest possible change. If several rules together produce an unwanted pattern, an entire part may need redesigning. State which relationships change together and why. Small changes can be easier to interpret, but that should not become a reason to leave a problem unresolved.

This draft first aligns the wording and placement of planks. Keep extra planks, rounds, and mechanisms with their separate proposals. Assemble one consistent set and ask someone new to start from setup, noting what still needs your explanation.
你不开口，材料能把一局讲清吗？
我们已经决定先澄清木板去向。下一步是把材料放到第一次接触的人面前，看看它能否自己说明怎样准备、行动和结束。设计者熟悉每一个细节，很容易觉得漏掉的句子“大家应该知道”；独立阅读会让这些脑中的补充重新变成需要写明的问题。
先给出这次真正要使用的完整材料。下面是基本版的 v0.3 材料草稿：玩法不变，整理了木板分区和动作说明。它尚未经过真人试玩。
一份足够从准备走到结束的材料
材料与摆放。准备小兔、小刺猬各一张纸片，二十张木板纸片，一个轮标和一个回合提示。纸上画四个依次相连的位置：“起点河岸—第一块踏脚石—第二块踏脚石—对岸”，并写出第1至第4轮。轮标从第1轮开始。回合提示先指向小林。
小林控制小兔，小雨控制小刺猬，两只动物都放在起点。画出三个放置区：中央“可用木板”放四张；“备用纸片”放十六张；“已用木板”开始为空。备用表示尚未取得的新木板，不能直接拿来支付前进；已用木板不再使用。
目标与次序。双方合作，必须两只动物都到对岸才算获胜，没有个人分数。最多四轮，每轮先小林、后小雨，每人一个回合。可以商量，各自决定自己动物的动作。
每个回合。从前进、收集和等待中选择一种允许的动作。前进需要中央至少一块可用木板：花一块放进已用区，把自己的动物向对岸移到下一个相邻位置，不能后退或跳格。收集只允许仍在起点的动物进行：从备用区拿两张新木板放入中央，动物不动，这个回合不能再前进。等待则不改变动物或木板，结束自己的回合。动物可以同处一格，不互相阻挡；已到对岸的动物在后续回合只能等待。
结束与换轮。每次动作完成后，双方都到岸就立刻共同获胜。否则，小林做完交给小雨；小雨做完后，若还没到第四轮，就把轮标向后移一轮，再轮到小林。第四轮双方都行动完仍未共同到岸，就共同失败。没有天气、捷径、借木板或其他能力。
二十张纸片已经够用：四轮共八个回合，即使每次都收集，也只需十六张备用。材料允许玩家摆出所有基本局面，无须临时找额外纸片。
材料完整，才知道哪里没讲通
实际进行这种测试前，参与者需要知道这是待修改的草稿，可以随时求助、暂停或停止。这个约定在开局前说清，不藏在游戏胜负规则里。也不要求他们为了测试坚持沉默。
接着可以让参与者自己摆放和阅读。设计者先留意他们在哪里查找、怎样解释动作、什么时候不能继续。如果主持者一开始就替大家分好三堆，还口头强调“只能拿备用”，之后便没有检查材料能否独立讲清这些事。
举一个假想情况：读者把二十张全放到中央。他可能没有注意到开局的四张，也可能把“备用”理解成随时能花。此刻看到的是准备环节的疑问，不是“四块初始木板已经太多”的证据。可以请他说明从哪句话得到这个摆法，再提供帮助。
若帮助之后继续，留下帮助发生的地方即可。后半局仍能帮助理解玩法，只是不能把整局称为完全依靠原材料完成。若规则缺口使人无法继续，也可以停止这次尝试，修订后再安排；到不了结尾本身就可能是有用发现。
能自行运行以后，还需要知道什么？
玩家若能独立摆好、完成动作、判断结束，说明这一次的材料支持了这些事情。它还不能证明每位新手都能读懂，也不能证明游戏值得反复玩。有人理解得很快却觉得安排单调，有人喜欢规划却需要更大的字。这些问题要继续分别观察。
当问题从“木板从哪里拿”变成“谁该留下收集”，你就可以开始关注两人怎样使用规则。保留这次使用的材料和收到的提问，下一位接手时才能沿着同一稿继续。
Can the Materials Explain a Game Without You Speaking?

We have chosen to clarify where planks come from and where they go. Next, we can give the materials to someone new and examine whether they explain setup, actions, and the ending. A designer knows every detail and can easily assume that “everyone will know” an omitted step. Independent reading exposes what the designer has been supplying from memory.

First, here are the complete materials for this attempt. This is the base game’s v0.3 materials draft. The play is unchanged; the plank areas and action instructions have been clarified. It has not yet been playtested with people.
Enough information to go from setup to ending

Materials and setup. Prepare one Rabbit piece, one Hedgehog piece, twenty paper planks, a round marker, and a turn reminder. Draw four connected spaces in order: “Starting bank—First stepping stone—Second stepping stone—Far bank.” Write rounds 1 to 4. Start the round marker on round 1 and the turn reminder pointing to Lin.

Lin controls Rabbit; Yu controls Hedgehog. Both animals begin on the starting bank. Draw three areas. Put four planks in the central “Available planks” area, sixteen in “Spare pieces,” and none in “Spent planks.” Spare pieces represent new planks not yet collected and cannot directly pay for movement. Spent planks cannot be used again.

Goal and order. Players cooperate and win only when both animals reach the far bank. There are no personal scores. Play for up to four rounds, with one turn for Lin followed by one turn for Yu in each round. Players may discuss plans, but each decides their own animal’s action.

On a turn. Choose one permitted action: move, collect, or wait. To move, at least one available plank must remain. Spend one by putting it in the spent area, then move your animal to the next adjacent space toward the far bank. You cannot move backward or skip a space. Only an animal on the starting bank may collect: take two new planks from the spare area and add them to the center. The animal stays still and cannot also move this turn. Waiting leaves animals and planks unchanged and ends the turn. Animals may share spaces and do not block each other. An animal on the far bank can only wait on later turns.

Ending and rounds. After each action, if both animals have arrived, players win together immediately. Otherwise, after Lin’s turn, pass to Yu. After Yu’s turn, if this was not round 4, advance the round marker and return to Lin. If both turns of round 4 finish without both animals arriving, players lose together. There is no weather, shortcut, borrowing, or special ability.

Twenty pieces are sufficient. Four rounds contain eight turns, so even collecting every turn requires only sixteen spare pieces. These materials can represent every base-game situation without finding extra pieces during play.
Provide complete materials before examining the gaps

Before this kind of test, participants should know that the draft is being revised and that they can ask for help, pause, or stop at any time. Explain that before play; do not bury it among the game’s victory rules. Participants are not required to remain silent for the test.

Then let them set up and read. The designer can watch where they look, how they interpret actions, and when they cannot continue. If the host sorts all three piles and explains “Take only from the spare area” first, the session has not examined whether the materials communicate those steps independently.

Imagine a reader placing all twenty planks in the center. They may have missed the four-plank setup or understood “spare” as something immediately available to spend. This reveals a setup question, not evidence that four starting planks are already too many. Ask which wording led to that arrangement, then provide help.

If play continues after help, record where it happened. The rest of the session can still inform our understanding of the game; the whole game simply cannot be described as completed entirely from the original materials. If a missing rule prevents continuation, the attempt can stop and be arranged again after revision. Failing to reach the ending may itself reveal something useful.
What remains after the game runs independently?

If players set up, act, and determine the ending independently, the materials supported those tasks on that occasion. This does not establish that every beginner will understand them or that the game invites repeated play. Someone may understand quickly but find the planning repetitive; someone else may enjoy planning while needing larger text. Those questions need separate attention.

When questions move from where to take planks to who should stay and collect, you can start examining how the pair uses the rules. Keep the materials and questions from this attempt so the next handoff can continue from the same draft.
别人接手时，怎样拿到同一款游戏？
朋友拿到了新地图，动作提示却还是旧的；说明写“收集新木板”，纸片旁边又写着“回收”。每个文件都在，合起来却不能让人确定到底该怎样玩。交接的第一件事，是让对方收到一套彼此一致的东西。
我们把这次要交出的过河草稿叫作“基本版 v0.3”。它仍是可以继续修改的原型。天气、捷径和其他讨论过的点子，各自属于比较用的方案，没有自动加入这个版本。
交出去的内容，必须足以开局和结束
这个版本需要两张动物纸片、二十张木板纸片、一个轮标、一个回合提示，以及下面这份地图与规则。它可以直接写在纸上，不需要专用软件或购买组件。
基本版 v0.3。地图是起点河岸、第一块踏脚石、第二块踏脚石、对岸，四处依次相邻。小林控制小兔，小雨控制小刺猬，两只都从起点开始。中央“可用木板”放四张，“备用纸片”放十六张，“已用木板”留空。轮标指向第1轮，回合提示指向小林。
最多四轮，每轮小林先、小雨后，各有一个回合，可以讨论，各自作决定。每回合选一种允许的动作：中央至少有一块时，花一块可用木板放进已用区，自己的动物向对岸前进到相邻位置；仍在起点时，可以改为从备用区收集两块新木板放入中央，动物不动；或者等待，不改变动物和木板。每种动作都用掉这个回合，不能收集后再前进。
不能后退或跳格，两只动物同处一格不阻挡。已经到岸的动物，后续回合只能等待。已用木板不再使用，备用纸片须经过收集才能成为可用木板。没有天气、捷径、个人分数、借用或特殊能力。
每次动作完成后，双方都到岸就立刻共同获胜。否则，小林做完轮到小雨；小雨做完后，若不足四轮，就推进轮标，再由小林开始。第四轮双方都行动完仍未共同到岸，就共同失败。四轮至多八次收集，所以十六张备用纸片足够。
这份说明和材料清单提供完整玩法。接手的人还应知道：若愿意参与试玩，可以求助、暂停或停止；这些选择不需要通过游戏里的投票，也不影响是否被认真对待。
版本差异，告诉别人哪里需要重新看
假设合作伙伴以前见过 v0.2。只告诉他“改得更清楚了”，他很难知道应当更换什么。针对本课程的版本示例，可以写明：v0.3 统一了三个木板区的名称，收集说明指出从备用区取两块新木板，前进说明明确已用木板不回流；人数、初始四块、每步花一块和四轮期限不变。
于是，对方知道应当把地图、规则和动作提示一起换成新版，而不是只换标题页。旧材料可以留作比较，但应标明旧版，避免开局时混在一起。若以后决定改成五轮，那就是玩法变化，还要重新准备足够的备用纸片，不能只改轮标上的数字。
一个短小的版本说明可以让后续讨论找到对象。“这个地方仍然看不懂”应当能对应到哪份说明，而不是大家各自在脑中想一个版本。重要变化和改动理由，也能让后来接手的人知道哪些选择值得重新考虑。
已经检查过什么，哪些仍不知道？
这个基本版已经做过按规则逐步推演的检查：存在双方成功的安排，也能确认某些安排会失败。例如双方第一轮都前进后，余下两块木板不够再走四步。这类检查支持规则下的数量和可能性判断。
课程中的玩家询问和试玩记录都是假想例子。我们还没有用这个材料版得到真人试玩结果，因此不能把它介绍成“新手已经看懂”“两人都很喜欢”或“可以放心出版”。纸上算得通，和陌生人能否使用、是否愿意再玩，需要不同证据。
下一位合作伙伴可以帮助检查第一次阅读，也可以提出新的玩法方向。接手设计并不只是润色字句；若发现共同过河缺少值得比较的安排，规则本身也可以继续修改。只是每次都应知道正在改变什么，以及已有结论是否仍适用。
把棋盘、规则和改稿说明放在一起，交给下一位玩家。你已经有一份能继续工作的草稿；对方开局时的一次停顿、一句询问，就可能给下一次修改指出方向。
How Can Someone Else Receive the Same Game You Intended?

A friend receives the new map but an old action reminder. The rules say “collect new planks,” while a label beside the pieces says “recycle.” Every file is present, yet the set does not tell them which procedure to follow. A handoff begins with materials that agree with one another.

We will call this crossing draft “Base game v0.3.” It remains a prototype that can change. Weather, shortcuts, and other ideas discussed in the course belong to separate comparisons. They have not automatically entered this version.
Provide enough to begin and finish

This version needs two animal pieces, twenty paper planks, a round marker, a turn reminder, and the map and rules below. These can be written on paper without special software or purchased components.

Base game v0.3. The map has four adjacent spaces in order: starting bank, first stepping stone, second stepping stone, far bank. Lin controls Rabbit and Yu controls Hedgehog. Both animals begin on the starting bank. Put four planks in the central “Available planks” area, sixteen in “Spare pieces,” and none in “Spent planks.” Start the round marker on round 1 and the turn reminder pointing to Lin.

Play for up to four rounds. Each round gives Lin one turn followed by one turn for Yu. Players may discuss plans but make their own decisions. On a turn, choose one permitted action. If at least one available plank remains, spend one by putting it in the spent area and move your animal to the next adjacent space toward the far bank. If your animal is still on the starting bank, you may instead collect two new planks from the spare area and add them to the center without moving. Or wait, leaving animals and planks unchanged. Each action uses the turn; collecting cannot be followed by movement on that turn.

Animals cannot move backward or skip spaces. They may share a space without blocking each other. An animal on the far bank can only wait on later turns. Spent planks cannot be reused. Spare pieces become available only through collecting. There is no weather, shortcut, personal score, borrowing, or special ability.

After every action, if both animals have arrived, players win together immediately. Otherwise, pass from Lin to Yu. After Yu’s turn, if this was before round 4, advance the round marker and return to Lin. If both turns of round 4 finish without both animals arriving, players lose together. Four rounds allow at most eight collect actions, so sixteen spare pieces are sufficient.

These instructions and the materials list provide the complete game. Anyone joining a playtest should also know that they can ask for help, pause, or stop. Those choices need no in-game vote and do not affect whether their contribution is taken seriously.
Explain changes so people know what to revisit

Suppose a collaborator has already seen v0.2. “I made it clearer” does not identify which materials to replace. For this course’s version example, we can be specific: v0.3 aligns the names of all three plank areas, tells players to collect two new planks from the spare area, and states that movement sends planks to a spent area from which they never return. Player count, the four starting planks, the one-plank move cost, and the four-round deadline remain unchanged.

The collaborator now knows to replace the map, rules, and action reminder together, rather than just a title page. Old materials can be retained for comparison but should be marked as old so they do not enter the next setup by accident. A later change to five rounds would change play and require enough spare pieces too; changing the number on the round track alone would be insufficient.

A short version note gives later discussion a clear object. “This part is still confusing” should refer to an identifiable set of instructions, rather than different versions in different people’s minds. Recording important changes and reasons also helps someone taking over understand which decisions might need reconsidering.
Say what has been checked and what remains unknown

The base rules have been examined through step-by-step rule analysis. There are successful plans, and some plans can be shown to fail. For example, if both animals move in round 1, the two remaining planks cannot pay for the four remaining moves. This kind of check supports claims about quantities and possibilities under the rules.

The player questions and playtest records in this course are invented examples. We have no results from real players using this materials version. It cannot yet be described as understood by beginners, enjoyed by both players, or ready for publication. A game that works in a paper calculation still needs different evidence about whether unfamiliar people can use it and want to play again.

A collaborator can help examine a first reading or suggest a new direction. Taking over a design may involve more than polishing sentences. If the shared crossing lacks worthwhile plans to compare, the rules can change too. Each time, we should know what is changing and whether earlier conclusions still apply.
Put the board, rules, and revision note together for the next player. You have a draft you can keep working on. A pause or question during their setup may give the next revision its direction.
还没读规则，你已经猜到了什么？
还没打开盒子，你可能已经猜这是一场比赛，或一段合作冒险。封面上的人物、标题里的动词，常常比第一条规则更早告诉人该期待什么。下面用一个虚构的邮局游戏，看看这个期待怎样影响开局。
设想一篇虚构故事：邮差岚独自冒雨翻山，把信送到灯塔。后来做成的桌游，盒面仍画着他一个人奔跑，宣传语仍强调“最快的邮差”；玩法却让大家共同经营邮局，没有个人送信排名。只看盒子的人，可能先把它想成一场比赛。
一幅画先给了一个方向
这个猜法并不一定来自粗心。孤身奔跑的人物与“最快”放在一起，容易让人期待速度和个人胜利。等讲解者说“你们共同完成任务”，他才需要调整刚才形成的理解。
期待也能帮助入门。知道自己是邮差，一张纸上的信封便像值得送达的东西。问题出现在图像与语言持续指向一种玩法，规则却要玩家做另一种事；新读者必须先纠正印象，才能继续学习。
把故事变成游戏时，可以选一个适合玩家行动的片段：为岚出发做准备、安排不同邮差的接力，或处理灯塔收到信以后的回程，都与独行送信有关，却提出了不同问题。选定共同经营邮局，就要让人看懂自己参与的是分派与交接，不能只靠重现那幅跑向灯塔的画面。
故事里的伙伴，桌上的信件
为了看清差别，只补一段交接规则：大家共同胜利，信件却放在当前持有者的邮差卡上。两位邮差必须在同一地点；持信者在自己的回合花一个行动，才能把一封信交给另一位。
现在岚和沐都在桥头，信在岚的卡上。轮到沐时，他可以提议接力，却不能直接拿走信件。需要等岚的回合，由岚花一个行动交出。这段是假想玩法里的一个片段，不是完整游戏。
“我们是一间邮局”说明双方的关系，“共同胜利”说明希望一起完成的结果，交接句子则说明眼前一封信怎样换人。合作不会自动让信件成为随时可拿的公共物品，故事里的默契也不会替玩家补出行动时点。
给最早的猜测一个回应
盒面的独行人物未必需要删掉。开场可以说：“那次岚独自送到了；这一局，你们安排整间邮局。”读者于是知道，熟悉故事与当前游戏之间有联系，也有变化。
接着把信放在角色卡上，展示桥头的一次合法交接，便把人物关系连到一个能看清的动作。开场介绍提供方向，具体例子补上谁持有、谁行动、什么时候能交。它们帮助彼此，不能互相代替。
只说“所有人齐心协力”还不够具体；一开始就列交接的每个例外，又可能让人忘记为什么要送信。介绍需要在两者之间搭桥：先给一个值得理解的目的，再把眼前的一步讲清。
熟悉故事，不等于替别人定规则
设想熟悉故事的玩家说：“岚绝不会把重要的信交出去。”这是他对人物的理解。另一位却可能觉得接力表示岚开始信任伙伴。两种说法都能讨论，规则仍然允许岚交信。
如果大家确实想尝试“岚不能交信”，就要明确说这是新约定，并在使用前共同同意。它取消了一个行动，可能影响邮局如何合作；不能把它藏在“懂故事的人都知道”里面，让不熟悉原作的人悄悄失去选择。
这样，新玩家也有位置提问：既然共同胜利，为什么信还要分持有人？这个问题可能帮助我们看见交接带来的会合安排，也可能指出说明尚不清楚。没读过原故事，并不妨碍他认真理解眼前这局。
熟悉故事还可能让某人更常发言。假设一位玩家能说出每个配角的名字，总把新朋友的计划称为“不懂邮局”。那些知识也许能带来有趣细节，却没有赋予他另一位玩家的行动权。介绍把眼前所需关系说完整，新朋友就能凭已知规则提出办法，不必先通过故事记忆的考验。
如果想让熟悉者分享，可以邀请他补一句人物背景，再把当前动作交还给正在行动的人。分享背景和主持别人的回合，是两件可以分开的事。
拿自己的封面或邀请文字做一次试读，先别解释玩法。听对方猜谁会赢、自己要做什么，再翻开规则看前几个动作。两处接不上的地方，就是标题、画面或说明值得修改的位置。
What Have You Already Guessed before Reading the Rules?

Before opening a box, you may already expect a race or a cooperative adventure. A character on the cover and a verb in the title can set expectations before the first rule. A fictional post-office game lets us follow that expectation into setup.

Imagine a fictional story in which the courier Lan crosses a mountain alone in a storm to deliver a letter to a lighthouse. A later board game still shows Lan running alone on its box and advertises “the fastest courier.” Yet its players jointly run a post office, with no individual delivery ranking. Someone looking only at the box may expect a race.
An Image Offers a Direction First

That guess need not come from carelessness. A lone runner combined with “fastest” readily suggests speed and individual victory. Hearing “you complete the task together” requires the newcomer to adjust an understanding already taking shape.

Expectations can also help someone begin. Knowing you are a courier can make an envelope on paper feel worth delivering. Trouble arises when images and words keep pointing toward one kind of play while the rules ask for another. The newcomer must correct an impression before learning can continue.

Turning a story into a game involves selecting a part people can act within. Preparing Lan’s departure, arranging relays between couriers, and handling the return after the letter arrives all connect with the solitary delivery while posing different problems. Choosing to run a post office calls for making assignment and handovers understandable, rather than only reproducing a picture of somebody running toward the lighthouse.
Partners in the Story, Letters on the Table

To see the difference, add only a handover rule. Everyone wins together, but a letter sits on its current holder’s courier card. Two couriers must be in the same location. The holder may spend one action on their own turn to pass one letter to the other courier.

Lan and Mu now stand together at a bridge, with the letter on Lan’s card. On Mu’s turn, Mu may suggest a relay but cannot simply take the letter. The handover must wait for Lan’s turn and cost Lan an action. This is a fragment of imagined play, not a complete game.

“We run one post office” describes a relationship. Shared victory describes the result everyone wants. The handover sentence specifies how one letter changes hands now. Cooperation does not automatically make letters public objects anyone can take, and fictional trust does not supply missing action timing.
Answer the Earliest Guess

The lone figure need not disappear from the box. An introduction could say, “Lan made that delivery alone. In this game, you organize the whole post office.” A reader can now recognize both a connection with the story and a change.

Placing the letter on a courier card and showing one legal handover at the bridge then connects that relationship to a visible action. The introduction gives direction; the example explains possession, the acting player, and timing. They support one another without performing the same job.

“Everyone works together” alone is too vague. Starting with every handover exception might instead bury the reason for delivering a letter. The introduction needs to connect them: offer a purpose worth understanding, then explain the immediate step clearly.
Knowing the Story Does Not Set Rules for Everyone Else
